text:
**Pick: B.** Converting $155,000 a year from Joyce's IRA in 2026–2031, while Frank is alive and they file jointly, leaves the most after-tax wealth.

I ran all three options through the full year-by-year projection. It used the stated conventions, Frank's death in 2032, Joyce filing single from 2033, and a 22% heirs' tax on IRAs. The wealth figures below are at the end of 2050, in 2026 dollars.

| Option | After-tax wealth | vs. C |
|---|---|---|
| C: No conversions | $3,072,664 | — |
| A: Convert 2033–2038 | $3,144,173 | +$71,510 |
| B: Convert 2026–2031 | $3,328,935 | +$256,272 |

**Why B wins**
- **Low brackets now.** In 2026–2031 their income is only Social Security, interest and tax-exempt interest. Without conversions their federal tax is about $1,000–$2,000 a year until RMDs start in 2031. The $155,000 conversions are taxed mostly at 22%, with the lower brackets filling first.
- **Single brackets after 2032.** Once Frank dies, Joyce files single, and the RMDs on Frank's large IRA push her into the 24% and 32% brackets and Medicare IRMAA tiers 3 and 4. Under C her federal tax runs $37,000 to $105,000 a year.
- **What B does to that.** Converting Joyce's IRA early shrinks her own RMDs. Her IRA falls to about $127,000 by 2050, against $969,000 under C. Lifetime federal tax is $332,977 lower than under C, and lifetime Medicare premiums are $46,004 lower.
- **Why A is weaker.** A converts at single-filer rates, with $147,000–$149,000 of RMDs on top of each $155,000 conversion. That puts them at about $82,000 of federal tax a year in the 24%–35% brackets, and in IRMAA tier 4 from 2035. The conversions are smaller in tax terms than B's and cost more per dollar converted.

Frank's own IRA is not converted in any option, and it keeps producing large RMDs for Joyce. The result is not a close call.

**N1.** 2026 federal tax is $33,282 under B and $1,041 under C, a difference of $32,241. B's extra income also raises taxable Social Security and shrinks the senior deduction.

**N2.** In 2028, Medicare premiums are set by 2026 income. Under B, 2026 MAGI is $259,476, which is IRMAA tier 1. Each spouse then pays $3,764 under B versus $2,558 under C. The difference is 2 × $1,206 = $2,412. Part D surcharges are included.

PICK: B
N1: 32241
N2: 2412

text:
**Answer: Option C is best.** Converting now beats waiting, and waiting beats not converting. I ran all three options through the full 2026–2050 projection with your conventions: 6% returns, 2.5% inflation, 10% heirs' tax, no state tax, and Medicare premiums set by income two years earlier.

**Why converting wins**
- **RMDs.** Ken's $970,000 IRA and Gail's $290,000 IRA are large. With no conversions, their RMDs push taxable income up every year, to about $360,000 of taxable income by 2050. Without conversions, income in the 2030s is high enough to land in the 22% and 24% brackets.
- **Smaller IRAs.** Each $65,000 converted shrinks Ken's IRA. That cuts later RMDs, and the income and tax that come with them, in every year from 2029 on.
- **The conversion rate.** Conversions are taxed at 12% and 22% now, plus the senior-deduction effect described below. The tax they avoid later is about 22% and up. The 10% heirs' tax on what remains in the IRAs also favors converting.
- **Pro-rata rule.** Part of each conversion is tax-free because of Ken's $131,000 of basis.
- **Medicare IRMAA.** Income stays below the first IRMAA tier in every option. Converting adds no Medicare surcharges, so lifetime Medicare cost is identical across options.

**Does converting cost them the senior deduction?** Yes, but only partly, and it's a small cost.
- **Option B.** Without a conversion, their income is under $150,000, so they get the full $12,000 ($6,000 each) in 2026–2028.
- **Option C.** Each $65,000 conversion lifts their income over the $150,000 phase-out line. The deduction falls by 6% of the excess for each spouse: from $12,000 to $9,693 in 2026, $9,246 in 2027 and $8,868 in 2028. That costs about $500–$700 of extra tax a year.
- **Option A.** Converting in 2029–2031 means they have already lost the senior deduction, because it expires after 2028. A therefore gives up nothing on the deduction, but it still starts later and does less overall.

The tool breaks down C's extra tax this way. In 2026 it is about $8,300 from the conversion itself, about $500 from the lost deduction, and about $855 from dividends pushed out of the 0% capital-gains band.

| Option | After-tax wealth at end (2026 dollars) | Compared with B |
|---|---|---|
| B (no conversion) | $3,170,788 | n/a |
| A (convert 2029–31) | $3,216,465 | +$45,677 |
| C (convert 2026–28) | $3,243,317 | +$72,529 |

C beats A by about $26,850, so the gap is well over the $1,000 "close" threshold.

**N1: 2026 federal tax, C versus B**
- Option C: $16,311
- Option B: $6,620
- Difference: **$9,691** more tax under C.

**N2: 2026 senior deduction under C**
- It is $9,693 for both spouses combined, down from $12,000 under B.

PICK: C
N1: 9691
N2: 9693

text:
**Pick: A.** It leaves the most after-tax wealth, but only by about $3,700 in 2026 dollars.

**How I ran it.** I ran all three options through the projection tool for 2026–2050 with your conventions. Those were 6% returns, 2.5% inflation, heirs taxed at 10% on traditional IRAs, and no state tax. I entered Glen's $144,000 IRA basis and the 2024 and 2025 MAGI figures. I also entered Glen's $28,000 pension, the $4,200 property tax, and both Social Security claims.

**Why converting helps only a little.** Without conversions, Glen's IRA grows to about $1.8M by 2050, and the RMDs push them into the 22–24% brackets and into a wide band of the Social Security "tax torpedo." Converting at 22–24% in 2026–2028 cuts lifetime federal tax by about $129,000. Part of that is offset because the conversions:
- remove the $12,000 senior deduction in 2026–2028, since MAGI goes far above $150,000;
- raise the taxable portion of Social Security;
- trigger the 3.8% net investment income tax;
- push 2028 Medicare premiums into the first IRMAA tier, which costs about $2,400 that year and in each of the next two years.

Net of those costs, the gain is small.

**A vs. B.** Option B's extra $5,500 a year is taxed at 24%, plus the net investment income tax and the extra Social Security taxation. That costs more than it saves later. B comes out $450 worse than doing nothing, and A comes out $3,704 better.

**After-tax wealth at the end, in 2026 dollars:**

| Option | After-tax wealth | vs. C |
|---|---|---|
| A | $2,516,844 | +$3,704 |
| B | $2,512,691 | −$450 |
| C | $2,513,140 | — |

A's lead over C is more than $1,000, so this is not a "CLOSE" call. It is a thin margin, though. Higher spending or a lower return would favor no conversion, and Glen dying early would shrink or erase A's lead.

**N1 (2026 federal tax, B minus C).** B owes $41,855 and C owes $4,665. The difference is $37,190.

**N2 (2028 Medicare premiums, B minus C).** Under B, 2028 premiums are set by 2026 MAGI of $270,305. That is in the first IRMAA tier (above $230,000), so each person pays $3,764 a year. Under C, each pays $2,558. For two people the difference is 2 × ($3,764 − $2,558) = $2,412.

PICK: A
N1: 37190
N2: 2412

**Result:** Option A leaves the most after-tax wealth. Option B is about $2,450 behind A, and both beat doing nothing.

| Plan | After-tax wealth at end of 2050 (today's dollars) | Versus no conversion |
|---|---|---|
| C: No Roth conversion | $2,364,915 | — |
| A: $190,000/yr, 2026–2028 | $2,427,431 | +$62,516 |
| B: $195,500/yr, 2026–2028 | $2,424,980 | +$60,065 |

Both conversions help because Glen's traditional IRA keeps growing and would otherwise drive large required distributions later, at higher brackets. Converting now moves money into the Roth at 22–24% rates while leaving room for the 2027–2028 conversions. A beats B by more than $1,000, so this is not a close call. B adds $5,500 more to the 2026 conversion, which pushes MAGI past the 24% bracket and into the higher IRMAA tier for 2028. That extra tax and premium cost outweighs the benefit of the additional conversion.

**N1: Federal income tax, 2026, B versus C.** Under C, 2026 federal tax is $4,665. Under B it is $41,855. The difference is **$37,190**. This comes from:
- $32,505 of extra tax on the $195,500 conversion, taxed at 12%, 22% and 24%.
- $257 more tax from Social Security becoming taxable.
- $2,880 lost to the senior deduction phase-out.
- $776 tax on qualified dividends, which are pushed out of the 0% band.
- $772 net investment income tax, since MAGI exceeds $250,000.

text:
**Pick: Option B** (convert $155,000 a year from Joyce's IRA in 2026–2031). It leaves about $3.31 million in after-tax wealth in today's dollars, versus $3.13 million for Option A and $3.05 million for Option C. That is about $186,000 more than A and $266,000 more than C, so it is not a close call.

**Why B wins**

- **Frank's death changes the tax picture.** Before 2032 they file jointly, with the wider brackets, the larger standard deduction, and the higher joint IRMAA thresholds. After Frank dies, Joyce files as single, so the brackets are narrower and the Medicare tiers are reached at lower income.
- **Required minimum distributions (RMDs) would otherwise spike.** Under C and A, 2032 RMDs from both IRAs push taxable income above $180,000, and from 2033 Joyce's single-filer income runs well into the 24–35% brackets. Under A, the 2033–2038 conversions are taxed at 24–35% and also push her into IRMAA tiers 3 and 4.
- **B moves money out of the IRA early.** Converting at 12–24% in 2026–2031 shrinks the IRA balance before the RMDs grow. Lifetime federal tax is about $0.94 million under B, versus about $1.27 million under C (nominal dollars, from the lifetime totals).
- **A's advantage over C is small.** A adds only about $80,000 over doing nothing, because it converts at the higher single-filer rates.

**Answers to the numbers**

- **N1 (2026 federal tax, B minus C):** Federal tax is $33,282 under B and $1,041 under C, a difference of $32,241 in the table. The tool's explanation of the change totals $32,240; I've used that figure, and the $1 gap is rounding. The increase is mostly the conversion itself (about $24,800), plus about $5,200 of extra taxable Social Security (the tax torpedo) and about $2,300 less senior deduction.
- **N2 (2028 Medicare premiums, B minus C):** Under B, 2026 MAGI of $259,476 puts both of them in IRMAA tier 1, so each pays $3,764 a year versus $2,558 under C. Two people give $2,412 more.

**Caveats**

- My first run entered Social Security as a future claim, which understated 2026 benefits ($56,732 instead of your $70,560). I reran with the benefits entered as already being paid. The ranking is unchanged, and the figures above come from the corrected run.
- The tool's sensitivity checks (7% return, heirs at 12%, longevity, spending of $90,400, Joyce claiming at 70) move the dollar results but do not change which option wins.
- Results assume 5% returns, 2.5% inflation, and Frank's death in 2032 as you specified.

PICK: B
N1: 32240
N2: 2412

text:
**Answer: Option C (convert $65,000 a year from Ken's IRA in 2026, 2027 and 2028) leaves Ken and Gail the most after-tax wealth.**

**Results (after-tax wealth at December 31, 2050, in today's dollars)**

| Option | After-tax wealth | vs. B |
|---|---|---|
| B: No conversions | $3,170,788 | — |
| A: Convert 2029–2031 | $3,216,465 | +$45,677 |
| C: Convert 2026–2028 | $3,243,317 | +$72,529 |

C beats A by about $26,900, well over the $1,000 closeness threshold, so this is not a close call. Lifetime federal tax is about $112,000 lower under C than under B. Medicare premiums are the same in all three options, because no IRMAA tier is crossed.

**Why C wins:** Ken's IRA is the only pre-tax account that the conversions draw on, and the required minimum distributions (RMDs) will grow later. Moving $195,000 out of the IRA now, at 12% and 22% rates, avoids larger RMDs later at higher brackets. Waiting until 2029–2031 (option A) gives up some of that benefit, because those years also carry larger RMDs.

**Senior deduction and the phase-out:** The $6,000 per-person senior deduction is reduced by 6% of MAGI over $150,000 for each spouse. Under C, 2026 MAGI is $169,221, so the total deduction falls from $12,000 to $9,693. The conversion costs them about $2,307 of deduction in 2026. That loss is small compared with the bracket cost, so it does not change the choice. The deduction also expires after 2028, which is why the 2026–2028 window matters.

**2026 federal tax:** Option B is $6,620 and option C is $16,311, a difference of $9,691. Most of that is the taxable part of the $65,000 conversion, plus tax on dividends and gains that the conversion pushes out of the 0% band.

**Caveats:** The projections use the stated conventions: 6% returns, 2.5% inflation, a 10% heirs' tax rate, and the joint brokerage account's titling left out. The follow-up checks show that a different return, a different life expectancy, or a different spending figure would change the dollar amounts. None of them changes which option is best among A, B and C.

N1: 9691
N2: 9693

PICK: C

text:
**Plan.** The best plan is to convert $118,000 a year for 8 years, from 2026 through 2033. I ran the full 2026–2050 projection with the conventions you gave. It applies:
- the Social Security "tax torpedo" (the extra tax on Social Security benefits as income rises);
- the senior deduction and its phase-out;
- the pro-rata rule for Ray's $208,000 of after-tax basis;
- IRMAA, set by income two years earlier;
- RMDs;
- the heirs' 12% tax rate.

That plan ends with about $134,400 more after-tax wealth, in 2026 dollars, than converting nothing.

- **Why not more.** Their income is low until RMDs start, so the first dollars converted are taxed at 12% to 22%. Above about $150,000 a year, the senior deduction phases out, more Social Security becomes taxable, and IRMAA starts. At that point each extra dollar costs about 22–24 cents, against the 12% the heirs would pay later. The results by amount per year, over 8 years, are:

| Amount per year | Gain, 2026 dollars |
|---|---|
| $100,000 | $127,000 |
| $110,000 | $132,000 |
| $120,000 | $131,000 |
| $150,000 | $112,000 |
| $200,000 | $110,000 |
| $300,000 | $73,000 |

- **Why 8 years.** Over 8 years the conversions drain most of Ray's traditional IRA's growth, which would otherwise be taxed through RMDs. The IRMAA-limited plans I tested did slightly worse, at roughly $112,000–$134,000.

**N1.** With no conversion, 2026 federal tax is $2,812. Converting $155,000 raises it to $30,488, so they owe $27,676 more. Three things drive the increase:
- The conversion is taxed at the 12% and 22% brackets.
- Taxable Social Security rises from $33,064 to $47,328.
- The senior deduction falls from $12,000 to about $2,984.

**N2.** The conversion lifts 2026 MAGI to $231,138. That is above the 2028 joint IRMAA threshold of $230,000, so both spouses land in tier 1 for 2028. Each person's annual premium is:
- With the conversion: ($298.50 + $15.20) × 12 = $3,764.
- With no conversion: $213.20 × 12 = $2,558.

The difference is $1,206 per person, or $2,412 for both.

PLAN: 118000 x 8
N1: 27676
N2: 2412

**Pick: B. Giving from Sam's IRA by QCD leaves them the most after-tax wealth.**

I ran each option through the full 2026–2050 projection. Option A is the facts as given. Option B has an $11,000 QCD from Sam's IRA every year, no checks, and $89,000 of spending.

**Why the QCD wins**
- The QCD counts toward Sam's required minimum distribution, which is $26,792 in 2026. The $11,000 therefore never shows up as income.
- Under A, the $11,000 gift is paid by check and the whole RMD is taxable. Because they take the standard deduction, only $2,000 of the gift gets a tax benefit.
- Lower income also means less of their Social Security is taxed. That is the extra benefit of the QCD.
- Their Medicare premiums are the same under both options.
- Final after-tax wealth in 2026 dollars:

| Option | After-tax wealth |
|---|---|
| A (checks) | $1,149,924 |
| B (QCD) | $1,261,282 |

B is ahead by about $111,000, so this is not a close call.

**N1: 2026 federal tax, B versus A**
- Option A's 2026 AGI is $106,033. The deduction is the $35,500 standard deduction plus the $2,000 charity deduction for non-itemizers, plus the $12,000 senior deduction. Taxable income is $56,533 and federal tax is $6,288.
- Option B's 2026 AGI is $87,340, since the QCD is excluded. The deduction is the $35,500 standard deduction plus the $12,000 senior deduction. Taxable income is $39,840 and federal tax is $4,285.
- The difference is $4,285 − $6,288 = −$2,003, so B owes $2,003 less.

**N2: taxable Social Security in 2026 under option A**
- Their total benefits are $62,640, and $49,352 of that is taxable.

PICK: B

N2: 49352

text:
**Pick: A.** Converting $260,000 a year in 2026 and 2027 leaves the most after-tax wealth. I ran all three options through the full 2026–2050 projection using your conventions.

**N1: Lou's 2026 RMD.** Lou was born in 1953, so his RMDs start at 73. The December 31, 2025 balance of $1,570,000 divided by the Uniform Lifetime Table factor of 26.5 gives **$59,245**. Edie's separate RMD on her $390,000 IRA is $14,717, so the household RMD is $73,962.

**How the RMD interacts with a conversion.**
- The RMD has to come out first, and it can't be converted. It is taxable income in its own right.
- Any conversion stacks on top of the RMD, Social Security (about $47,000 of it taxable in 2026), dividends and interest.
- Under B, 2026 income is low enough that they keep the full $12,000 senior deduction. Federal tax is only $11,350.
- Converting phases out the senior deduction (6% of income over $150,000). That adds a hidden tax cost in the first years of conversion.
- Converting also moves capital-gain and dividend income out of the 0% band and triggers the 3.8% net investment income tax for a couple of years.

**Results (after-tax wealth at the end of 2050, in 2026 dollars):**

| Option | Change vs. B | Lifetime federal tax | Lifetime Medicare premiums vs. B |
|---|---|---|---|
| B (RMD only) | baseline, $3,084,611 | $872,744 | baseline |
| A | **+$110,943** | $650,357 | +$11,450 |
| C | +$103,782 | $709,219 | −$3,324 |

- **A** pays about $75,400 of federal tax in 2026 and $73,500 in 2027, with income reaching the 24% bracket.
  - Its 2026 income of about $416,000 triggers Medicare surcharges in 2028 and 2029 (IRMAA tier 3), costing about $19,700.
  - It then shrinks the IRA enough to cut later RMDs and taxes by roughly $8,000 to $30,000 a year. Tax in the late 2040s is much lower, and the IRMAA tier that B reaches in 2049–2050 is avoided.
- **C** stays in the 22% bracket but takes six years, with a smaller IRMAA surcharge and a smaller shift of money out of the IRA.
- A beats C by about $7,200 and beats B by about $111,000, both well above the $1,000 "close" threshold.

**N2: 2026 federal tax, C versus B.** C's 2026 tax is $29,873, against $11,350 for B. The difference is **$18,523**. About $15,800 of that is tax on the $75,000 conversion. About $2,000 is the senior deduction shrinking from $12,000 to $3,002. About $700 is extra tax on dividends and gains.

One sensitivity: the tool reran the result at a 3% return, and C would then beat A. At the 5% return you specified, A wins.

PICK: A
N1: 59245
N2: 18523

text:
**Recommendation: convert $118,000 a year for 8 years (2026–2033).**

**How I got there.** I set up the household as described, with Ray and Linda as the two people on Medicare, both Social Security benefits at full retirement age, and the $208,000 after-tax basis in Ray's IRA. I then ran the solver over flat annual amounts for up to 10 consecutive years, and it chose $118,000 for 8 years. Compared with doing nothing, that adds about $134,000 of after-tax wealth in today's dollars at 2050, measured with the IRAs net of the heirs' 12% tax. Converting $118,000 keeps 2026 MAGI around $199,000, which avoids any IRMAA surcharge in the years that matter, so lifetime Medicare cost does not change.

The runner-up options were close. A $110,000 a year plan gains about $132,000, and a plan that stays under the first IRMAA tier each year gains about $134,000 to $133,900 (the solver's "stay under the first IRMAA tier" option). The solver still ranked $118,000 a year first, and it did not flag a close call.

**The $155,000 test (N1 and N2).**
- **N1:** The 2026 federal tax with the $155,000 conversion is $30,488, against $2,812 with no conversion. The difference is **$27,676**. That is the 12% and 22% bracket tax on the conversion, plus about $3,138 from more Social Security becoming taxable, less about $1,984 of senior deduction lost to the MAGI phase-out.
- **N2:** 2026 MAGI rises to $231,138, just above the 2028 joint tier-1 threshold of $230,000. Each spouse's 2028 premium goes from $2,558 (Part B $213.20 plus no Part D surcharge, times 12) to $3,764 (Part B $298.50 plus Part D $15.20, times 12). Both spouses together add **$2,412** a year.

**Sensitivity.** The plan depends on the stated conventions. The solver's follow-ups show that a 7% return would shift the best plan to $180,000 a year for 8 years, and heirs at a 32% bracket would shift it to $220,000 a year. Those are not the conventions you specified, so I used the 5% return and 12% heirs' rate.

PLAN: 118000 x 8
N1: 27676
N2: 2412

text:
**PICK: C.** Option C leaves the most after-tax wealth. I ran all three options through the full projection from 2026 to 2050, using the conventions you gave. Each option was run against Sam and Pat's whole household: both Social Security benefits, the pension, interest, dividends, Medicare premiums with the two-year lag, and RMDs on every traditional account. The projection ran to 2050 because no deaths were specified.

**N1.** The 2026 RMD on Pat's inherited IRA is $510,000 ÷ 20.9, which is about $24,402. The parent died after their required beginning date, so annual RMDs apply during the 10-year window. The divisor is Pat's single-life-table factor for age 65 in 2024 (22.9), less one for each year since.

**Why C comes out ahead.** The RMD is the same in every option, so the options differ only in when the rest comes out.
- **A:** The extra $200,000 in each of 2026 and 2027 pushes AGI to about $349,000 and $353,000. That is taxed at 22–24%. It also wipes out the $12,000 senior deduction and triggers the 3.8% net investment income tax in those years. The inherited IRA is nearly empty afterward.
- **B:** Taking only the RMD keeps 2026–2032 cheap, with taxes of roughly $11,000–$40,000 a year. But the whole remaining balance (about $553,600) lands in 2033. That year's AGI is about $812,000, and much of the income is taxed at 32–35%. It also pushes Medicare premiums into a higher IRMAA tier in 2035.
- **C:** The extra $55,000 a year spreads the withdrawals across eight years. It mostly stays in the 22–24% brackets. It avoids both A's spike and B's 2033 bunching, and it does not push the IRMAA tier as high.

After-tax wealth at the end, in 2026 dollars:

| Option | After-tax wealth |
|---|---|
| A | $4,686,489 |
| B | $4,708,755 |
| C | $4,721,638 |

C beats B by about $12,900. That is more than the $1,000 "close" margin, so this is not a CLOSE call.

**N2.** Federal income tax for 2026 is $24,520 under C and $10,755 under B. C is $13,765 higher.

PICK: C
N1: 24402
N2: 13765

**Answer: Option A leaves the most after-tax wealth, by about $5,100 over Option C. The 2026 RMD is $59,245.**

**Lou's 2026 RMD.** Lou turns 73 in 2026, so the RMD starts this year. Using the 12/31/2025 balance of $1,570,000 and the Uniform Lifetime divisor of 26.5 gives $59,245. Conversions made on December 31 don't change this figure. Edie also turns 73 and has her own RMD of $14,717 on her $390,000 IRA, which the projection includes.

**Results.** Each option was run through 2050 under the stated conventions, with after-tax wealth in 2026 dollars:

| Option | After-tax wealth | Versus B |
|---|---|---|
| B: RMD only | $3,136,919 | — |
| A: $260,000 a year in 2026–2027 | $3,234,225 | +$97,306 |
| C: $75,000 a year in 2026–2031 | $3,229,093 | +$92,174 |

A beats C by $5,132. That is more than the $1,000 close-call band, so the answer is A, not CLOSE. The margin is small, though. The sensitivity check found that at a 3% return instead of 5%, C would edge out A. The 5% convention is what the question specifies.

**Why A does well.** Both conversion options use the same 2026 RMD and Social Security, and they fill the 24% and 32% brackets with conversions. Option A moves more money into the Roth in two years. Because the 2028–2029 conversion stops, it avoids several later years of conversions, which keeps the Roth-to-IRA balance favorable for heirs. Option A's IRMAA cost is higher, though. Under A, Lou and Edie move into IRMAA tier 3 in 2028 and 2029 because of 2026 income, which costs about $7,400 per person per year in Medicare premiums.

**N2: 2026 federal tax, C minus B.** Under B, 2026 federal tax is $11,350. Under C, it is $29,873. The difference is $18,523. Most of it comes from the $75,000 conversion taxed at 12% and 22%. The senior deduction shrinks from $12,000 to $3,002 as MAGI passes $150,000.

**Caveats.** The brokerage account's titling was not given. The tool did not flag it as changing the decision, so I left it out.

text:
**Answer: Option C (the Roth conversion) leaves Frank and Joyce with the most after-tax wealth.**

**The 0% gains room is smaller than it looks.** Under doing nothing (B), their 2026 taxable income is $51,744, which leaves about $47,000 of room under the $98,900 0% threshold. Option A realizes $110,000 of gains, so only about $47,000 of it can be taxed at 0%. The rest is taxed at 15%, and the 2026 tax on dividends and gains rises by $11,343. Option A also pushes up the taxable portion of Social Security (the "tax torpedo") and shrinks the senior deduction. Its 2026 federal tax rises by $12,876, and its end-of-plan wealth falls by about $24,500 (in today's dollars) versus B.

**The conversion costs more tax now but comes out ahead.** Option C moves $110,000 from Frank's IRA to his Roth. Because $172,000 of his IRA is after-tax basis, only about $88,500 is taxable under the pro-rata rule. That adds about $17,191 to 2026 federal tax, through the 12% and 22% brackets plus the same torpedo, senior-deduction and gains effects. Over the plan, though, the Roth growth and smaller future RMDs leave them about $39,600 (today's dollars) ahead of B. That is about $36,000 more than option A, and it is the largest of the three.

**Results (after-tax wealth at end of plan, today's dollars):**
- B, Neither: $3,163,771
- A, Realize $110k gains: $3,139,293
- C, Convert $110k to Roth: $3,203,401

**Sensitivity:** The follow-up checks changed the size of the advantage but not the ranking. A higher or lower return, a different heir tax rate, an earlier death for Joyce, or higher spending each left C as the best option. The gap is well over $1,000, so this is not a close call.

text:
**Result: Option C leaves the most after-tax wealth.** The projection runs each plan through 2050 with the stated conventions (6% return, 2.5% inflation, heirs taxed at 32% on inherited pre-tax IRAs).

| Plan | After-tax wealth (2026 $) | vs. B |
|---|---|---|
| B: RMD only, rest in 2033 | 4,708,755 | — |
| A: extra $200k in 2026 and 2027 | 4,686,489 | −22,266 |
| C: extra $55k a year, 2026–2033 | 4,721,638 | +12,884 |

**Why C wins.** Pat's inherited IRA must be empty by 2033, so Plan B leaves a large forced withdrawal in 2033. The model shows about $553,600 coming out of that IRA that year, pushing taxable income to about $770,000 and the federal tax bill to about $195,000. Spreading the withdrawals across 2026–2033 keeps them mostly in the 22% and 24% brackets. It also avoids the 2033 Medicare surcharge spike, which adds IRMAA costs for two years at the high tiers. Plan A front-loads $200k into 2026–2027. That lands in the 32%–35% brackets and triggers IRMAA tier 2 in 2028, so it comes out behind B.

**Inherited IRA RMD for 2026.** The required minimum is $24,402, based on the $510,000 year-end 2025 balance. Because the parent had reached the required beginning date, annual RMDs continue during the 10-year window.

**Federal tax, C vs. B in 2026.** Federal tax is $24,520 under C and $10,755 under B, a difference of $13,765. Under C, the extra $55,000 of withdrawals is taxed mainly at 12% and 22%, and the senior deduction shrinks by $6,494.

**Sensitivity.** The decision holds under the follow-ups the tool ranked. Muni interest, a higher return, or spending changes move the wealth figure but not the choice. C beats B by about $12,900, which is well above the $1,000 "close call" threshold, so the pick is C and not a tie.

**Assumptions I made.** Pat's Roth contribution basis was not given, so I left it out; it only matters if Roth money is spent, which the model does last. The brokerage account's titling was not given either; it matters only at a death, and none falls in the projection.

PICK: C

text:
**Pick: C, converting $110,000 from Frank's traditional IRA to his Roth in 2026.** I ran all three options through the full 2026–2050 projection. I used 6% returns, 2.5% inflation, no state tax, and a 24% heirs' tax on traditional IRAs.

**Why neither "room" is free**
- Without either move (B), their 2026 income is low. Social Security, the pension, dividends and interest give an AGI of about $99,000, a taxable income of about $51,700, and federal tax of $4,790. Their MAGI for IRMAA is $119,000, which is well below the first IRMAA tier. They also get the full $12,000 senior deduction.
- The 0% capital-gains band goes up to $98,900 of taxable income. That leaves roughly $47,000 of room, not $110,000.

**Option A: realize $110,000 of gains**
- Federal tax for 2026 rises from $4,790 to $17,666, an increase of $12,876.
- About $11,300 of that is capital-gains tax, because the gains spill past the 0% band into the 15% band.
- The rest comes from more Social Security becoming taxable and a smaller senior deduction.
- The extra income also pushes 2026 MAGI above the first IRMAA tier. That raises their 2028 Medicare premiums by about $2,400.
- The higher cost basis saves only small amounts of tax later. Over the full plan, A ends $24,478 worse than B in 2026 dollars.

**Option C: convert $110,000**
- Federal tax for 2026 rises from $4,790 to $21,981, an increase of $17,191.
- The conversion is only partly taxable, because Frank's $172,000 of after-tax basis is recovered pro rata. The taxable part is about $88,500.
- MAGI for IRMAA stays below the first tier, so there is no Medicare surcharge.
- Moving money into the Roth shrinks Frank's traditional IRA. That lowers the RMDs and the tax on them from 2035 on, and the IRA left to heirs is smaller.
- Lifetime federal tax falls by $48,575. C ends $39,630 ahead of B in 2026 dollars.

**Result in 2026 dollars, after heirs' tax:**

| Option | After-tax wealth | Versus B |
|---|---|---|
| A | $3,139,293 | −$24,478 |
| B | $3,163,771 | — |
| C | $3,203,401 | +$39,630 |

C is best, and the gap to the next option is far more than $1,000.

One fact in the problem looks inconsistent. Frank, born January 1960, has a full retirement age of 67, which he reaches in 2027. He therefore couldn't have claimed at full retirement age by 2026. I used the stated $3,500 a month, since the tax calculations depend on the benefit amount and not on the claiming age.

PICK: C

text:
**Pick: C.** Sam claims at 70, Pat claims at 67, and they convert $180,000 a year from Sam's traditional IRA in 2026–2029. I ran all three options through the full year-by-year projection with your conventions. Sam's death in 2040 applies to every option, and the plan runs through 2050.

**After-tax wealth at the end, in 2026 dollars:**

| Option | After-tax wealth | Versus A |
|---|---|---|
| A: both claim at 67 | $2,625,461 | – |
| B: Sam at 70, Pat at 67 | $2,641,584 | +$16,123 |
| C: B plus the conversions | $2,812,226 | +$186,765 |

**Why waiting until 70 helps, but only a little (B vs A).**
- Sam's benefit is about 24% larger from 70. After he dies in 2040, Pat's survivor benefit is the larger of the two, so the bigger check lasts for the survivor's years.
- Waiting costs some money early. Savings fall faster, which means less taxable interest.
- B also pays about $30,000 more lifetime tax and about $6,000 more in Medicare premiums than A. More of the benefit is taxable later, and there are higher IRMAA tiers for the survivor.
- Those costs eat most of the gain.

**Why the conversions are worth it (C vs B).**
- While Sam delays Social Security and before RMDs start, their taxable income is very low. Without conversions it is roughly zero, so the low brackets go unused.
- Converting $180,000 a year in 2026–2029 fills the 10%, 12% and 22% brackets at a cost of about $20,000–$25,000 a year in federal tax.
- That lowers the traditional IRA balances that RMDs are later taken from. RMDs are smaller, and later-year taxable Social Security and tax are much lower.
- The survivor, filing single after 2040, also avoids the higher IRMAA tiers. The Medicare premium difference is a Part B and Part D IRMAA effect.
- Lifetime federal tax falls by $211,748 and Medicare premiums by $32,267.

**N1.** In 2026, option B owes $0 in federal income tax. Standard deduction plus the $12,000 senior deduction exceed their income. Option C owes $22,255. The extra tax is about $20,374 on the conversion, $1,139 from the senior deduction phasing down, and $743 on dividends moving out of the 0% band. The difference is $22,255.

**N2.** Under option B, Sam claims at 70 in 2030 and gets a 3.6% COLA in 2027 and 2.5% after that. His 2031 benefit is $59,376. This is his 2031 total for the year, from the projection.

The results depend on a few inputs. They include spending of $112,000 a year, the 6% return, and the 10% heirs' tax rate. The tool flagged that a higher spending level (about $134,400 a year) could make B the best option instead. At the stated $112,000, C is clearly best.

PICK: C
N1: 22255
N2: 59376

**Why this can't be answered reliably**

Both questions ask which fund will actually do better in the Roth IRA by 2036. That depends on future market returns, and no one can know those. The planning conventions give every account the same 6% return, so under them the two options are identical.

Here is how the two funds compare on the factors that are knowable:

- **Taxes inside the Roth:** A Roth IRA has no yearly tax on dividends or gains, and qualified withdrawals are tax-free. The high-dividend fund's larger payouts therefore cost nothing extra in tax inside the Roth. The tax-efficiency edge that a total-market fund has in a taxable account doesn't apply here.
- **Dividends:** Dividends stay in the Roth and are reinvested. A dividend payout isn't extra return. The share price drops by the amount paid.
- **What does differ:** Total return depends on the fund's holdings, sector concentration, fees and market conditions over the period. The conventions assume none of this, and history doesn't reliably favor either fund over a 10-year span.
- **Fees:** Costs can be checked. Index funds usually charge less, which is a small, known advantage for A, but the size is unknown without the actual expense ratios.
- **Conversion size:** Neither fund changes the $100,000 conversion, its tax, or the Medicare premium effects. Those are set by the conversion itself and not by what is bought afterward.

Under the 6% convention for every account, the 2036 Roth value is the same for A and B, so the difference is $0. That figure comes only from the convention and says nothing about which fund will actually perform better.

text:
**Option B (QCD) leaves them more after-tax wealth.** Projected to 2050, in today's dollars:

- **A (checks):** $1,149,924
- **B (QCD):** $1,261,282
- **Difference:** about $111,000 in favor of B, far more than the $1,000 closeness threshold.

**Why B wins**

- **Pre-tax money leaves at full value.** A $11,000 QCD takes pre-tax IRA money that would otherwise be worth only 76 cents on the dollar to heirs (after their 24% tax). Each check, by contrast, comes from cash at full value.
- **Lower taxes in 2026.** The QCD is excluded from income, and it counts toward Sam's 2026 RMD. Under A, the $11,000 check gets only the $2,000 non-itemizer deduction, so the standard deduction ($35,500 with both 65+) still applies and the check adds nothing else. Under B, the QCD cuts taxable income and the taxable share of Social Security.
- **Lower taxes in later years too.** Because the IRA shrinks by $11,000 a year, later RMDs and the taxable share of Social Security are lower. Lifetime federal tax falls from $359,091 under A to $336,153 under B.

**2026 figures under A (checks)**

- Social Security: $62,640 total (Sam $45,480, Pat $17,160).
- Ordinary income: Sam's RMD $26,792 (about $24,563 taxable after his $62,000 basis), Pat's RMD $14,118, savings interest $13,500 (5% of $270,000), Pat's interest $4,500.
- Tax-exempt interest of $7,000 counts toward Social Security taxability but not income tax.
- AGI $106,033; taxable income $56,533; federal tax $6,288.
- Taxable Social Security is $49,352. Check: provisional income is $95,001 (AGI excluding Social Security $56,681, plus $7,000 tax-exempt, plus half of benefits $31,320). Taxable amount = 85% of the excess over $44,000 ($43,351) plus $6,000, which gives about $49,351.

**2026 figures under B (QCD)**

- AGI $87,340; federal tax $4,285.
- The 2026 difference is −$2,003.

**Caveats**

- Medicare IRMAA is zero in 2026 and 2027 under both options, since the 2024 and 2025 MAGIs are below the joint thresholds. Under A, MAGI rises to $136,000–$150,000 range later, which triggers surcharges; B's lower income keeps more years below the thresholds.
- I assumed both claimed Social Security at FRA 66, as the facts imply. I used the tool's figures for everything else.

PICK: B
N1: -2003
N2: 49352

**Short answer:** The planning conventions can't tell you which fund will actually do better. They give both options the same 6% return, so under them the Roth ends up identical either way.

**Why the conventions produce a tie**

- Every account earns 6% a year in the model, whatever it holds. So option A and option B produce the same Roth balance.
- The Roth's contents don't change anything else in the plan. Dividends inside a Roth are not taxed, so the high-dividend fund's 2% yield creates no tax cost or tax benefit. Federal tax, IRMAA, Social Security taxation and the spending withdrawals all come out the same under both options.
- The $100,000 conversion, its tax, and the spending waterfall are identical in both options.
- So under the conventions the 2036 difference is $0.

**Why that doesn't answer "which will actually do better"**

- The facts give no return estimates, fees or volatility for either fund. The only return in the model is the 6% planning assumption, which applies to both.
- In reality, a high-dividend fund and a total market index fund can differ in total return (price plus dividends), expense ratio, and sector mix. None of these is in the facts, so any real-world ranking would be a guess.
- Scale matters. Each 1 percentage point of annual return gap compounds to roughly 10% of the Roth balance over ten years. On a Roth of about $160,000 after the conversion, that is on the order of $15,000–$25,000 by 2036. That is the size of the real-world question, and it depends on return forecasts the facts don't supply.

**What would settle it:** each fund's expected total return, its expense ratio, and the return assumption you want to test, if you want to model a return gap. With those, the same model could compare the two options under different returns.

PICK: CANT

text:
**Recommendation: Option C.** Sam claims at 70, Pat at 67, and they convert $180,000 a year from Sam's traditional IRA to his Roth in 2026–2029. It leaves about $2.81 million in today's dollars, versus $2.64 million for B and $2.63 million for A. C beats B by about $171,000, far outside the $1,000 closeness band.

**What drives the result**

- **Delaying Sam to 70 helps only a little (B vs. A, +$16,000).** His benefit rises about 24% at 70, but the extra Social Security adds taxable income, and the "tax torpedo" makes more of it taxable in the early years. Without conversions, their income stays low until the IRAs force large RMDs, so the delay is worth little on its own.
- **The conversions do the heavy lifting (C vs. B, +$171,000).** Sam's IRA is $1.15 million. Without action, RMDs starting at 75 push taxable income to roughly $190,000–$330,000 a year after Sam's 2040 death. The survivor is then in the 24%–35% brackets with much of the IRA still unconverted. Converting $180,000 a year in 2026–2029 moves about $620,000 of pre-tax money into the Roth at 12%–22% rates, and the IRA balance is much smaller when RMDs begin.
- **Lifetime federal tax falls sharply.** Under C it is about $370,000, versus about $613,000 under B. Medicare premiums also fall, since the IRMAA surcharges are triggered less often later on.
- **Conversions don't trigger IRMAA surcharges.** Joint MAGI stays under the first IRMAA threshold in 2026–2030, so the 2028–2032 premiums are unchanged.

**Answers to the numbers**

- **N1 (2026 federal tax, C minus B): $22,255.** Under B, 2026 income is about $37,200 (interest, dividends, no Social Security), and the standard deduction and senior deduction bring taxable income to zero, so the tax is $0. Under C, the taxable part of the conversion is $155,931 (the rest is a nontaxable return of the $163,000 after-tax basis, by pro-rata). That puts taxable income near $150,807. The tax is about $20,374 on ordinary income plus $743 on qualified dividends at 15%, for $22,255 in total.
- **N2 (Sam's 2031 Social Security under B): $59,376.** He claims in February 2030 at 70 (about 124% of his $3,490 PIA), and the 2027 COLA of 3.6% plus 2.5% a year after that applies. The 2031 figure is 12 months of about $4,948.

**Caveats**

- The joint brokerage titling wasn't given. The model assumed a basis step-up at Sam's death. Community-property titling would change the result by about $6,000, but would not change the choice.
- The spending sensitivity ($134,400 a year) would reverse the ranking and make B best, but you gave $112,000, so I used that.
- Heirs at a 10% rate, a 6% return, and Sam's 2040 death are as you specified.

PICK: C
N1: 22255
N2: 59376

text:
**Answer: Option A (convert $135,500 in 2026) leaves the most after-tax wealth.**

**Set-up.** I ran the three options through the full 2026–2050 projection using the stated conventions: 6% growth, 2.5% inflation, 32% heirs' rate on pre-tax IRAs, and no deaths before 2050. Savings interest is taxable at 6% of the opening balance, and the $24,000 muni interest is tax-exempt but counts toward IRMAA MAGI. Both spouses claim the standard deduction, since $6,000 of property tax does not beat it.

**Results (after-tax wealth, today's dollars):**
- C, no conversion: $3,328,602
- A, convert $135,500: $3,389,555 (+$60,953 vs C)
- B, convert $126,500: $3,386,455 (+$57,853 vs C)

A beats B by about $3,100, which is more than the $1,000 closeness threshold, so this is not a close call.

**Why A wins.** The 2026 conversion fills the 12% bracket and most of the 22% bracket. Its cost is a bit more than B's, but the extra $9,000 converted now avoids larger IRA distributions later, when RMDs would push them into the 22% and 24% brackets. The Social Security torpedo and the senior-deduction phase-out add cost in 2026, and those costs are included in the figures above.

**N1 (2026 federal income tax, A minus C).** Federal tax is $28,456 under A and $2,964 under C, a difference of $25,492 from the year table. The tool's breakdown headlines the difference as $25,493, a one-dollar rounding gap. I used the tool's breakdown figure. The breakdown is: $21,415 from the conversion in the 12% and 22% brackets, $1,971 from more Social Security becoming taxable, $1,782 from the smaller senior deduction, and $324 from capital-gain tax.

**N2 (2028 Medicare, A minus C).** The 2028 premiums are set by 2026 MAGI.
- Under A, 2026 MAGI is $241,505, above the 2028 joint tier-1 threshold of $230,000. Each spouse pays $3,764 a year ($298.50 Part B + $15.20 Part D, × 12), or $7,528 for the couple.
- Under C, 2026 MAGI is $102,490, which is the standard tier. Each spouse pays $2,558 a year, or $5,116 for the couple.
- The difference is $2,412.

**Sensitivity.** The result depends on the return assumption. At a 4% return, B would beat A by about $38,900, so the choice between A and B is sensitive to returns. The 6% convention you specified favors A. The tool's other flagged facts (heirs' bracket, spending level, health, itemizing, basis in the IRAs) change the wealth totals but not the ranking. The brokerage account's titling does not matter here, since no death is modeled before 2050.

PICK: A
N1: 25493
N2: 2412

Option A leaves them the most after-tax wealth. I ran all three options through a year-by-year projection from 2026 to 2050 using your conventions.

**How I set it up**
- The projection used 6% returns, 2.5% inflation and a 32% heirs' tax rate on traditional IRAs.
- Walt's $46,000 of after-tax basis is handled with the pro-rata rule. His IRA is about $1,144,800 on December 31, 2026, after growth. So about 4% of any conversion is tax-free, and a $135,500 conversion adds $130,055 of taxable income.
- The muni interest is included. It is not in AGI, but it counts toward how much Social Security is taxable and toward the MAGI that sets Medicare premiums.
- Without a conversion, 2026 MAGI is about $102,490, which sits in the standard Part B tier.

**What a 2026 conversion does**
- It raises income into the 22% bracket, which brings more tax on the conversion itself.
- It makes more Social Security taxable, rising from $44,590 to $53,550.
- It shrinks the $6,000-per-person senior deduction, which falls from $12,000 to $3,899.
- It pushes 2026 MAGI to about $241,505 under A and $232,867 under B. Both are over the $230,000 level that sets 2028 Medicare premiums, so both trigger the first IRMAA surcharge in 2028.
- Option A costs $25,493 more federal tax in 2026 than C. Option B costs $23,364 more.
- Over time the conversion pays off. Smaller required distributions from Walt's IRA cut tax in 2032 and later, and the Roth money grows tax-free.
- Converting also keeps them out of the higher IRMAA tier in 2046–2048.

**Results (after-tax wealth at the end, in 2026 dollars)**

| Option | Change vs. C |
|---|---|
| A: convert $135,500 | +$60,953 |
| B: convert $126,500 | +$57,853 |
| C: no conversion | baseline |

A beats B by about $3,100, which is more than the $1,000 "close" margin. The extra $9,000 converted costs only the 22% bracket rate. It does not cross into a new IRMAA tier beyond the one B already triggers.

**N1:** 2026 federal tax is $28,456 under A versus about $2,964 under C. The projection reports the difference as $25,493, and I used that figure.

**N2:** 2028 Medicare premiums are set by 2026 MAGI. Under A, each spouse pays $3,764 (Part B plus Part D surcharge), or $7,528 together. Under C, each pays $2,558, or $5,116 together. The difference is $2,412.

PICK: A
N1: 25493
N2: 2412
